entries.name: Root cellar
entries.purpose: frost-free underground food storage before refrigeration
layout: rectangular room 3-5 m across
set into a north-facing slope or under the farmhouse
ventilation openings at floor and ceiling level for airflow
door faces away from the prevailing weather
entries.found: almost every pre-refrigeration farm in temperate zones; still common on old homesteads
entries.notes: Holds a steady 5-12 C through the year. The underground building nearly everyone dug once: frost never reaches it, so apples, potatoes and turnips overwinter there.

entries.name: Wine cellar
entries.purpose: long-term wine storage and ageing
layout: long gallery following the hillside contour
barrels at the far, coolest end
air circulates but drafts at the door are kept small
behind or beneath the wine-press house
entries.found: under wineries across southern Europe, the Rhine, Douro and Bordeaux; Georgian qvevri cellars are UNESCO-listed
entries.notes: Georgia's qvevri culture (buried clay egg-jars, ~8,000 years of wine) is the deepest-rooted wine storage; Loire and Savoie villages stack cellars four levels deep into tufa.

entries.name: Ice house (ice well)
entries.purpose: overwintering ice blocks for summer cooling, before mechanical refrigeration
parts: deep cylindrical pit or domed chamber
layout: cylindrical chamber 3-5 m deep and wide
loaded through the roof hatch in winter
meltwater drains away, cold air pools at the bottom
often partly below grade with walls thick with chaff
entries.found: estates, coaching inns and fish markets across cool Europe and North America from the 17th to the early 20th century
entries.notes: The coldest room in the village. On the north side of a house or buried in a bank, with the thatch 1 m thick; a good one kept food cold into August.

entries.name: Cistern
entries.purpose: underground storage of drinking water for dry seasons and sieges
layout: rectangular or circular room several metres deep
fed by roof catchment or aqueduct
stairs spiral down to the waterline
a cool ~10 C inside, always
entries.found: every city with irregular rainfall since antiquity; Istanbul alone preserves dozens of Byzantine ones
entries.notes: The greatest surviving example is the Basilica (Yerebatan) Cistern, Istanbul: 140 x 70 m, 336 columns, ~100,000 m3, built by Justinian I c. 532.

entries.name: Sewer tunnel
entries.purpose: drainage and waste removal
layout: gradient around 0.5% toward the outfall
mains deep, laterals shallow
vent points to street level
combined storm and waste until the modern era
entries.found: under every modern city; Rome's Cloaca Maxima (6th c. BCE) still drains the Forum to the Tiber
entries.notes: The Cloaca Maxima was 3.2 m wide and 4.3 m high, vaulted in stone and still in use; Pliny the Elder called it one of the marvels of Rome.

entries.name: Deep-level subway station
entries.purpose: mass rapid transit beneath dense city streets
layout: platform 10-30 m below street level
bored tunnels ahead and behind the hall
vent shafts rise into public squares
shallow cut-and-cover stations have a box mezzanine
entries.found: every dense metropolis; the deepest are Arsenalna (Kyiv, 105 m) and North Korea's deep stations doubling as shelters
entries.notes: Two builds: shallow cut-and-cover boxes (wide, flat) and deep bored tubes (curved walls). London's deep-level tubes are the classic circular bore.

entries.name: Hardrock metal mine
entries.purpose: extraction of gold, silver, copper, lead, zinc and tin ores
parts: vertical shaft with headframe and hoist
layout: shaft drops 300-3000 m
levels spaced every 50-100 m
adits at valley level for drainage and access
stopes worked back up from the bottom level
entries.found: mountain ranges and shields worldwide; Rudna Glava (Serbia) excavated copper ~5000 BCE, among the oldest known mines
entries.notes: The classic adventure-dungeon underground: shafts, drifts, adits and stopes. Abandoned ones are unstable, oxygen-poor and legally off-limits.

entries.name: Salt mine
entries.purpose: extraction of halite (rock salt)
parts: salt chapels and statuary in old mines
layout: chamber-and-pillar layout following salt beds
chambers 5-12 m high on multiple levels
pillars absorb overburden load, creeping slowly shut
dry, stable, ~10 C year-round
entries.found: under southern Poland and Austria; Wieliczka worked since the 13th century: 287 km of galleries, 9 levels, 327 m deep
entries.notes: Wieliczka is a dripping-works cathedral of rock salt, carved by miners over 700 years; Hallstatt (Austria) has mined salt since the Bronze Age. Salt mines are the safest large voids on earth.

entries.name: Underground coal mine
entries.purpose: extraction of coal seams
layout: seams 0.5-6 m thick followed along the strike
longwall panels retreat toward the shaft
methane drains via return (gob) airways
roof bolted or arched, never left naked
entries.found: coal measures worldwide: Appalachia, Wales, Poland, the Donbas, Shanxi, the Sydney Basin
entries.notes: The archetypal 19th-century Satan-pit: crouching galleries, black dust, pit ponies, cage shafts, and the constant fear of firedamp (methane).

entries.name: Underground quarry (carriere)
entries.purpose: extraction of building stone, lime and gypsum
parts: pillars left unmined for roof support
layout: grid of pillars and rooms tracking the best beds
chambers 5-10 m high under 20-40 m of overburden
Some galleries later used as ossuaries or mushroom farms
entries.found: under Paris (about 300 km of galleries, the stone of Notre-Dame and the Louvre), under Dover (chalk), under Malta (globigerina)
entries.notes: Half of Paris stands on its own quarry; collapses in 1774 swallowed a street and forced the creation of the Inspection des Carrieres.

entries.name: Qanat (karez, falaj)
entries.purpose: gravity-fed irrigation from mountain aquifers without pumps
layout: aligned shafts marching in a straight line downhill
tunnel drifted by hand at a gradient under 0.1%
shafts used for spoil, air and maintenance
outlet (mazhar) at the village edge
entries.found: Iran (~36,000 still working), Afghanistan, Oman (aflaj), Morocco, Algeria, Spain (Granada, Madrid), Sicily
entries.notes: The longest surviving is the Zarch qanat (~71 km); the Gonabad (Qasabeh) qanat is ~2,700 years old, 33 km long, mother well ~300 m deep, still flowing ~150 L/s. UNESCO 'The Persian Qanat' (2016).

entries.name: Pit dwelling (semi-subterranean house)
entries.purpose: dwelling; warm in winter, cool in summer
layout: pit 3-6 m across sunk ~1 m below grade
roof timbers pitched from the pit lip
smoke escapes a ridge hole or vent
door faces the sheltered side
entries.found: Jomon Japan (from ~11,000 BCE), Neolithic Europe, Norse Greenland, Seneca villages, forest-steppe Siberia
entries.notes: The evolutionary step between tent and house: the ground itself is the insulation. Thousands of excavated pit-house hollows survive in the archaeological record.

entries.name: Dugout (prairie/opal-mining dugout)
entries.purpose: frontier cheap dwelling; modern survival in desert towns
parts: room excavated into a bank or hillside
layout: one or two rooms cut into a coulee or spoil heap
the bank is three of the walls
roof poles laid across, turfed over
door facing south or east
entries.found: US and Canadian prairies 1860-1900; today Coober Pedy, Australia, where over half the town lives underground
entries.notes: Coober Pedy digs homes into opal-mine spoil: ~23 C inside year-round against 40+ C summer peaks. Hotels, churches and a museum are all dugouts.

entries.name: Troglodyte (rock-cut) dwelling
entries.purpose: dwelling and stable cut into soft rock
layout: chambers ring an open court sunk below grade, or line a cliff face (Guadix, Cappadocia)
kitchen, stable and store adjoin
ground surface is the roof
ventilation via courtyard and flues
entries.found: Matmata and Chenini (Tunisia), Cappadocia, Guadix and Sacromonte (Spain), China's Loess Plateau (yaodong), Coober Pedy
entries.notes: Tens of millions of people on the Loess Plateau may still live in yaodong cave dwellings (figures vary widely). The apex form is Derinkuyu: see underground_city.

entries.name: Cappadocian underground city
entries.purpose: communal refuge and habitation during raids
layout: levels connected by staircases 6-25 m apart
each level sealed independently by rolling doors from inside
ventilation shafts never line up between levels
kitchens and wine presses up top, chapel deepest
entries.found: Nevsehir Province, Turkey; ~200 Byzantine-era underground complexes known, most shallow; Derinkuyu is deepest
entries.notes: Derinkuyu: 8 excavated levels to ~85 m (40 m to the entry shaft, 85 m to the water shaft; '18 levels' is popular myth), population up to ~20,000, rediscovered 1963. Kaymakli and others interconnect by tunnel.

entries.name: Rock-cut tomb
entries.purpose: royal or elite burial
layout: long straight axis descending into bedrock
chambers off the corridor
shafts and turns defeat tomb robbers
burial chamber under the hill's highest point
entries.found: Valley of the Kings (KV62 Tutankhamun, KV5 with 120+ rooms), Petra (Urn and Palace Tombs), Lycian cliff tombs, Cerveteri
entries.notes: New Kingdom tombs run 60-200 m deep; the bent axis and descending corridors were deliberate anti-theft engineering.

entries.name: Catacomb
entries.purpose: underground burial place
layout: streets of niches stacked floor to ceiling
cubicula along main corridors
2-4 levels deep
communal galleries, chambers for the rich
entries.found: Rome (60+ named sites, ~600 km of galleries, 2nd-5th c.), Paris (Tombe-Issoire, 1786, ~6 million remains, 1.5 km ossuary route), Naples, Syracuse, Malta
entries.notes: Named from 'ad catacumbas' on the Appian Way. Paris's is half quarry, half ossuary: the bones were emptied from overflowing cemeteries by night, cartloads at a time.

entries.name: Crypt (undercroft)
entries.purpose: burial beneath a church; relic storage
layout: directly below the apse or choir
aisle chamber under thechancel above
columns rise to the chancel floor
family vaults along the sides
entries.found: most large European churches; Westminster Abbey, St Peter's Basilica, Austrian dynastic churches
entries.notes: The coldest, dampest, most echoing room in a church. The dead really are under the feet of the living; in candlelight the vault seems to breathe.

entries.name: Hypogeum
entries.purpose: prehistoric subterranean sanctuary and necropolis
layout: upper level scooped from a hill brow
middle and deep levels fully rock-cut
daylight reaches only the middle level via a small opening
lowest chamber 10.6 m below grade
entries.found: Malta (Hal Saflieni, c. 4000-2500 BCE, ~7,000 burials); comparable Maltese temple undergrounds
entries.notes: The only prehistoric underground labyrinth in Europe, carved with stone and antler, not metal; its 'Oracle Room' gives a voice uncanny carrying power.

entries.name: Mithraeum
entries.purpose: underground temple of the Mithras mystery cult
layout: dug below grade, often in a cistern or cave
benches along the long walls for reclining initiates
bull-slaying relief faces the entrance at the far end
initiation feast held inside
entries.found: Rome (dozens mapped), Dura Europos (Syria, 241 CE), under Bloomberg's London HQ, along Hadrian's Wall
entries.notes: Always dark, low and claustrophobic by design: the entire cult happened in candlelight. Around 680 Mithraea are known from across the Roman world.

entries.name: Kiva (Anasazi/Pueblo ceremonial room)
entries.purpose: ceremonial gathering; axis between underworld, earth and sky
layout: round room dug 1-1.5 m below grade
roof at plaza level, on 4 posts (great kiva) or ring beam
ladder down through the roof hatch
ventilator tunnel enters from the south side
blueprint: legend: # stone wall, s sipapu (ceremonial shaft), d south ventilator/entrance, . air
entries.found: American Southwest and Mexican Northwest; great kivas ~15 m across at Chaco Canyon; still built and used by modern Pueblo peoples
entries.notes: Family kivas are 3-5 m; Chaco great kivas reached ~15 m (Chetro Ketl ~19 m; Casa Rinconada 20 m). The sipapu is a deliberate little hole into the underworld.

entries.name: Painted cave (Upper Paleolithic art cave)
entries.purpose: ceremonial/shamanic art galleries; practical use unknown
layout: narrow passages opening into high halls
animals painted on the best-lit wall surfaces
art often invisible until a lamp is raised
generation upon generation added layers
entries.found: Lascaux (France), Chauvet (France, ~36,000 BP), Altamira (Spain), Cueva de las Manos (Argentina); ~350 decorated caves known
entries.notes: The world's oldest continuous art gallery. Painted by torchlight in total darkness, tens of thousands of years ago, likely by candlelit ritual.

entries.name: Souterrain (Iron Age refuge)
entries.era: Iron Age to early medieval (about 500 BCE-500 CE)
entries.purpose: food storage and refuge during raids
layout: narrow zigzag passage 1-2 m high
tight squeezes defeat an intruding attacker
terminates in a small chamber
hidden entry near the farm or refuge mound
entries.found: Gaul (thousands known), Scotland ('earth houses'), Ireland, Brittany, the Low Countries
entries.notes: Likely part grain store, part panic room: the best-preserved (e.g. Rennibister, Orkney) were cut into rock or corbelled under a mound.

entries.name: Fogou (Cornish underground passage)
entries.purpose: ritual, storage or refuge; purpose debated
layout: long low zigzag passage driven into a mound
walled then buried under an earth mound
entry through the courtyard of an adjacent house
stone-faced, deliberately claustrophobic
entries.found: Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly; ~50 known (Carn Euny, Chysauster, Chun Castle)
entries.notes: The interior acoustics and absolute dark are the point as much as the function; whether pantry, church or bunker is unresolved.

entries.name: Earth-sheltered house (modern)
entries.purpose: low-energy dwelling; passive solar plus earth coupling
layout: built into a south-facing slope
fully bermed or buried with a courtyard atrium
earth holds 10-16 C year-round
sun charges the mass by day, releases it at night
entries.found: Taos Eco-village (Earthships), Welsh co-ops (CAST/Caer Sidi), Norwegian turf houses (older cousin), passive-solar estates worldwide
entries.notes: The pit dwelling reborn with solar glazing and code compliance; survivable without any machines, by design.

entries.name: ICBM missile silo (Titan II type)
entries.purpose: intercontinental ballistic missile launch
layout: missile stands on a fire-protected pad at silo bottom
closure door slides open fully in 17-20 s
control capsule ~1 km away, blast-isolated
equipment terminal shares the blast envelope
entries.found: US missile fields (North and South Dakota, Nebraska, Kansas, Wyoming, Colorado, Washington); Soviet sites (Kazakh steppe, Ukraine)
entries.notes: Titan II silo: ~45 m deep, ~17 m across; the 740-tonne lid could blow open in 20 seconds. Many survive as museums (e.g. the Titan Missile Museum, Arizona).

entries.name: Hardened command bunker (Cheyenne Mountain type)
entries.purpose: hardened military command and control surviving nuclear attack
parts: horseshoe main chamber 45 x 18 x 180 m
layout: long entry tunnel dog-legged to defeat blast wave
main cavern crossed by four cross-caverns
buildings float on springs, touching no rock
redundant power, water and ventilation inside
entries.found: Cheyenne Mountain (Colorado, ~600 m of granite overburden, operational 1966); Swiss Warna bunkers, Albanian shelter system, British Regional Seats of Government
entries.notes: The hardest underground ever built: designed to keep functioning through a multi-megaton burst 1.5 NM away. Albanian dictator Hoxha built ~750,000 concrete bunkers, mostly small and shallow.

entries.name: Fallout (civil defence) shelter
entries.purpose: survival of nuclear strike and fallout
layout: built into a basement slab or behind an earth berm
single room or two-room with airlock
ventilation hand- or motor-driven
marked on the outside door
entries.found: Switzerland (legally required in every new building since 1963), Sweden, the US (1961-65 school and suburb drills), Soviet housing blocks
entries.notes: The single most common state-mandated underground structure of the 20th century; in Switzerland nearly every cellar has its taped hatch. Many were quietly converted to wine or cheese cellars.

entries.name: Limestone solution cave (karst cave)
entries.purpose: natural void: drainage route and habitat
layout: passages follow bedding planes and joints
big entrance at the valley rim, passages dive below
lower levels flooded (phreatic loops)
some halls exceed 100 m high (Sarawak Chamber)
entries.found: every limestone region: Kentucky (Mammoth Cave, 685 km surveyed), Slovenia (Postojna), China (Shuanghedong 480 km), Belize (ATM), Madagascar
entries.notes: The default 'big cave' on Earth. Mammoth Cave is the longest known cave system anywhere: more than 685 km of surveyed passage beneath limestone ridges.

entries.name: Lava tube
entries.purpose: solidified volcanic conduit (now void)
layout: nearly straight tube following the slope
multiple stacked levels where successive flows overlapped
entrance often a collapsed skylight trench
twisting braids where branches ran parallel
entries.found: Hawaii (Kazumura Cave: 65.5 km, 1,100 m descent, ~1500 CE), Iceland (Surtshellir), Lanzarote, Saudi Arabia, Venus and Mars (postulated)
entries.notes: Born in one eruption. Kazumura passages run up to 21 m wide and 18 m high; Nāhuku (Thurston Lava Tube) is its famous walkable sibling.

entries.name: Cenote (limestone sinkhole well)
entries.purpose: natural surface access to groundwater; Maya ritual sinkhole
parts: conduit linking to flooded cave systems
layout: circular pit 20-60 m across
cliffs drop 20-70 m to water
underwater passages connect cenotes into vast systems (Ox Bel Ha, 541 km)
entries.found: northern Yucatan Peninsula, Mexico, in a limestone plain with no rivers; thousands are known
entries.notes: Sacred Cenote (Chichen Itza): 60 m wide, ~27 m of sheer cliff to water; the Maya threw jade, gold and people to the rain god Chaac.

entries.name: Sea cave (wave-cut cavern)
entries.purpose: coastal erosion void
layout: entrance faces the open sea
floor sits at mean sea level
tapers to darkness inland
blow holes vent spray vertical metres above
entries.found: every rocky coastline: the Blue Grotto (Capri), Fingal's Cave (Staffa, basalt columns, ~70 m deep), Australian surf coasts
entries.notes: Fingal's Cave is a natural nave of basalt columns 22 m high, 72 m long, where the Atlantic breathes through. Timing visits with low tide matters.

entries.name: Ice cave (glacier cave)
entries.purpose: seasonal or perennial void in ice
parts: equilibrium line (perennial ice only if cold air pools)
layout: one of two types: valley-mouth limestone cave with an ice plug, or an ice tube inside a glacier
air drains downhill and pools, keeping ice in summer
Eisriesenwelt entrance is ~20 m wide and 18 m high, with 134 m of descent
entries.found: Austrian Alps (Eisriesenwelt, 42 km, largest ice cave, ~0 C), Iceland (Vatnajokull), the Alps, Alaska
entries.notes: Eisriesenwelt forms ~1 m of new ice every year; 1,400 steps lead ~1 km into the lit section of 42 km of passages. The ice is always rearranged.

entries.name: Asphalt (tar) seep
entries.purpose: natural asphalt seep; Pleistocene fossil trap
layout: small warm pools on level alluvial plain
deposits reach 4.5-10.6 m thick
seeps since ~60,000 years ago, still active
entries.found: Los Angeles (La Brea; >3 million fossils, 40,000-8,000 BP), Trinidad (Pitch Lake), Azerbaijan, Iraq (Hit), Peru (Talara)
entries.notes: La Brea is the richest Pleistocene fossil site known: mammoths, sabre-tooths, dire wolves, bison, camels. Chumash and Tongva used the asphalt to caulk canoes.

entries.name: Rabbit warren
entries.purpose: burrow complex of a rabbit colony
layout: 10-100 entrances clustered over a mound or bank
tunnels 0.5-1 m down, up to ~3 m
communal chambers deep; single holes shallow
escape runs branch toward cover
entries.found: Western Europe and North Africa; introduced to Australia, New Zealand and Chile as a farmed and game species
entries.notes: Romans spread the rabbit through Europe as farmed meat; post-medieval England legally reserved warrens for the gentry until enclosures collapsed.

entries.name: Badger sett
entries.purpose: European badger clan den territory
layout: clan territory with one main sett plus subsidiary setts
branching tunnels 1.5-4 m down
entrance mounds and flattened latrine runs mark it
communal sleeping chamber at depth
entries.found: Britain and Ireland, Western and Central Europe, Scandinavia, parts of NW Asia
entries.notes: Main setts are continuously occupied for centuries; some have 50+ entrances and house dozens of badgers across generations.

entries.name: Prairie dog burrow (town)
entries.purpose: burrow of black-tailed prairie dog colonies
layout: burrow 0.3-4.3 m deep and 10-30 m long
1-3 entrances per family coterie
hundreds to thousands of burrows in a 'town'
mounds serve as flood defence and lookout
entries.found: shortgrass plains of North America; 19th-century towns covered millions of hectares
entries.notes: Black-tailed prairie dog towns are 'the Serengeti of North America': ~100+ vertebrate species shelter in and around them, including the endangered black-footed ferret.
